# Changes for package `inventory`

## 1. `orders.go` — make `Reserve` atomic (critical, correctness)

Add a check-and-decrement method on `Store` in `store.go`, e.g.
`func (s *Store) Take(sku string, n int) bool`, that holds `mu` across the
entire read-modify-write (`if s.counts[sku] < n { return false };
s.counts[sku] -= n; return true`). Then rewrite `Reserve` in `orders.go` to
call `s.Take(sku, n)` instead of the separate `s.Get(sku)` followed by
`s.Add(sku, -n)`, returning `ErrOutOfStock` when `Take` returns false
(keep the existing package-level `Reserve` signature so the exported API is
unchanged). Reason: `Reserve` currently releases the lock between `Get` and
`Add`, so concurrent calls can both observe the same count and oversell,
driving stock negative (the comment in `orders.go` even documents this).

## 2. `store.go` — clamp `Add` so counts cannot go negative

Change `func (s *Store) Add(sku string, n int)` to refuse or clamp
`n` such that `s.counts[sku] + n < 0` (e.g. return a bool or clamp to
zero), or at minimum make all decrements go through the checked `Take`
method from change 1. Reason: `Add` is an exported method with no
validation, so any caller (or a negative `n` passed to `Reserve`, since
`Get(sku) < n` passes for `n < 0`) can produce negative inventory.

## 3. `report.go` — use `strings.Builder` in `Report`

Change `Report` to accumulate into a `strings.Builder`
(`sb.WriteString(fmt.Sprintf(...))` / `sb.WriteString(...)`) and return
`sb.String()` instead of `out +=` on a plain string. Reason: repeated
`+=` on a `string` allocates and copies the buffer on every iteration,
making the report O(n²) in the number of skus.

## 4. `orders.go` — validate `n` in `Reserve`

Have `Reserve` reject `n <= 0` (returning an error) before calling the
store. Reason: as written, a negative `n` passes the `s.Get(sku) < n`
check and silently *adds* stock, so `Reserve` can function as an
unauthenticated restock.

## 5. Add tests (new file, e.g. `orders_test.go`)

Add a test that hammers `Reserve` concurrently with `t.Parallel()`-style
goroutines and `sync.WaitGroup` asserting the count never goes negative
and the number of successful reserves is exact, plus a basic test of
`Reserve`/`Restock`/`Report`. Reason: nothing in the package pins down
the invariants from changes 1–4, and the race in change 1 would be caught
immediately by `go test -race` on such a test.

## 6. Minor: doc comments

Add doc comments to the exported items that lack them: `New` in
`store.go`, `Add` in `store.go`, and `Restock` in `orders.go`
(`ErrOutOfStock` and `Reserve`/`Report`/`Store` are already fine).
Reason: exported API items without doc comments get flagged by
`golint`/staticcheck and hurt the package's maintainability.

# Where the locking responsibility should live

**Commitment: inside `Store`.** Callers should only ever see atomic
operations; they should never see a lock. `mu` stays unexported, and every
compound behavior of this package (reserve, future transfer, future
bulk operations) is one method on `Store` that acquires and releases the
mutex in a single function.

## The argument

### 1. Invariants belong to the data, and only the data's owner can protect them

The invariants this package wants — (a) no oversell, (b) counts never
negative, (c) mutations consistent under concurrency — are all facts
about the `counts` map. "Check-then-decrement is atomic" is a rule about
which *sequences* of operations are legal on that map. If `Store` exposes
only `Get` and `Add`, it guarantees each is safe individually but says
nothing about their composition — and composition is precisely the part
that is not safe. A type whose exposed primitives compose into
invariant-violating sequences has a contract it cannot fulfill: either it
shouts "callers, beware" in comments (which is exactly what `orders.go`
does today), or it adds the atomic compound operation. The latter is the
fix, and it can only live where the map lives.

### 2. Callers cannot even express the discipline correctly

`mu` is unexported, so caller-side atomicity is not a matter of
discipline — it is impossible without a new API. To make it possible,
`Store` would have to export `mu` or a `Lock`/`Unlock` pair. That inverts
ownership: the type must now trust that *every* caller pairs
lock/unlock. `sync.Mutex` is not reentrant, so while a caller holds the
lock, every existing method (`Add`, `Get`) deadlocks if touched — the
type would have to document "never call these while holding," a contract
it cannot enforce mechanically. A forgotten unlock on an early return,
or a double lock, is now a caller bug that wedges the store for every
other goroutine in the process. In the committed design, pairing is one
`defer` inside a method that the caller cannot split apart.

### 3. The alternative's cost scales with operations × call sites

If callers own atomicity, every future compound operation (reserve with
hold, transfer between SKUs, multi-SKU bulk reserve, compare-and-set)
must be re-derived with its own interleaving risk at *every* call site,
and every reviewer must re-verify it. Defined once as a method on
`Store`, the cost is linear in the number of distinct operations, and
amortizes to zero at call sites.

### 4. It is the Go idiom, and the tooling enforces only this shape

The standard library is uniform on this: types protect their own state
with unexported mutexes and expose atomic operations, never locks
(`sync.Map`, `bytes.Buffer`, `time.Timer`). Linters treat exported
mutexes as a design smell. Go offers no way to mechanically verify that a
caller-side critical section covers the right range; the only
mechanically checkable structure is "each acquire/release pair lives in
one function, in the owner of the data."

### 5. Testability follows the same line

`Store.Take` is unit-testable in-package: `go test -race` with concurrent
hammering proves the invariant against the type itself. Caller-side
composition must be retested at every call site, and a missing test at
one site is a shipped race.

## What the caller-side alternative costs

1. **The `Reserve` race is the cost, already paid.** Two concurrent
   `Reserve` calls both pass `s.Get(sku) < n`, both execute
   `s.Add(sku, -n)`: oversell and negative stock, in code whose comment
   documents the race. That is what caller-side composition produces
   when nobody is positioned to make it right.
2. **The API required to make it possible is itself a hazard.** An
   exported mutex or lock pair invites forgotten unlocks and
   non-reentrant deadlocks, and converts a local logic bug into a
   process-wide stall of the store. In the committed design, the worst a
   buggy caller does is produce a logic bug.
3. **The invariant cannot be enforced at the primitive level either.**
   `Add` accepts any `n`, so `Add(sku, -10000)` is a perfectly
   "atomic" caller-side call that violates no-negative-counts. The
   caller-side API presents every individual operation as safe; the only
   unsafe thing is the *combination*, which is the worst possible signal
   — the unsafe path looks like the boring one.
4. **The tax is permanent and invisible in code.** Every future caller
   must know that two individually-locked calls are not atomic. That
   knowledge lives in heads and comments, not in the type signature, so
   it is lost every time a person or a module leaves.

## The counterargument, honestly

Caller-side composition has a real claim: `Store` stays a dumb general
keyed counter, and business policy (which SKUs may be reserved, how
holds and refunds interact) belongs in an upper layer. The price of the
committed position is that `Store` grows a method per compound
operation and accumulates domain vocabulary — a surface-area and review
tax. And if a rule ever genuinely spans data that isn't in one store (a
transfer across two `Store`s), no in-`Store` lock can express it anyway;
the answer then is to partition the data or add a higher-level
coordinator that owns *that* lock — not to export these locks.

I accept the surface-area cost, because it is the cheaper side of the
exchange: a new `Store` method is one small, testable, un-misusable
function; a new caller-side compound operation is an unverified
interleaving of shared mutable state at an arbitrary site.

## Escape hatch (does not change the commitment)

If a genuinely caller-owned compound operation ever appears, add a
scoped callback:

```go
// Update runs fn inside a single critical section on this store.
// fn sees the raw counts; it owns the read/write, Store owns the section.
func (s *Store) Update(fn func(counts map[string]int) error) error {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	return fn(s.counts)
}
```

The lock's lifetime never leaves `Store`, and because `fn` receives the
raw map rather than locked methods, reentrant deadlock is impossible.
Even so, prefer a named atomic method (`Take`) for any rule the store
owns, because the call site reads as one act and the invariant has a
name a test can reference.

## Bottom line

Locking — and the atomic operations built on it — lives in `Store`:
add `Take(sku string, n int) bool` in `store.go`, shrink `Reserve` in
`orders.go` to a thin wrapper over it, and keep `mu` unexported forever.
The caller-side alternative costs exactly what this package already
shipped: a documented race in the hot path, an API surface that can
deadlock or wedge the store, an invariant enforced only by convention,
and a review tax that never amortizes.
